- [PREFERENCE] The user has always been interested in martial arts.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Someone with a physical disability can practice martial arts, but adaptations may be necessary depending on the specific disability and martial art.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] For someone with a lower limb amputation, adaptations may include modifying stance and footwork, strengthening core muscles, and relying on upper body for balance.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Individuals with visual impairments may need to rely on touch cues or verbal instructions from a coach or training partner.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Individuals with mobility impairments may need to modify techniques or use equipment such as a wheelchair or prosthetic device.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Adaptive martial arts programs are available and may offer modified techniques and equipment to support individuals with disabilities.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] It is important to consult with a knowledgeable instructor and healthcare professional to determine the best approach for an individual's specific needs.
- [USER] The user expressed uncertainty about participating in martial arts due to their wheelchair.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Recommendations for adaptive martial arts programs include:
  1. Adaptive Martial Arts Association (AMAA) - a directory of adaptive martial arts programs.
  2. Karate for All - provides martial arts classes to children and adults with disabilities, including those who use wheelchairs.
  3. American Taekwondo Association (ATA) - offers "ATA Tigers" program for children with disabilities.
  4. Adaptive Martial Arts Academy - offers online martial arts classes and resources for individuals with disabilities.
  5. Wheelchair Martial Arts Association (WMAA) - promotes martial arts programs for individuals who use wheelchairs.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] It is important to do research and find a program that suits specific needs and interests, and to consult with a healthcare professional before starting any new physical activity.
